title: Earth's Wobbles and the Ice Ages
objective: After this level you can explain how slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt (Milankovitch cycles) pace the ice ages.
summary: Slow cycles in Earth's orbit shape, tilt and wobble decide how warm northern summers are. When they're cool, snow survives and ice sheets grow, as seafloor shells confirmed in 1976.

cards.headline: Earth wobbles like a spinning top, and the ice ages keep time with it.
cards.body: Level 76's ice core showed a slow beat of cold and warm. The metronome turns out to be Earth's own orbit.

items.label: Obliquity
points: The tilt of the axis, 22.1° to 24.5°

items.label: Precession
points: A wobble of the axis, like a top

cards.headline: It's all about summer
cards.body: Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovitch, born in 1879, asked which season matters most. His answer: summer in the far north. When those summers run cool, less of the winter's snow melts, and it piles up year after year into ice sheets. Growing ice then reflects more sunlight back to space, cooling things further, so a small nudge can grow.

mascot.line: Keep this: ice sheets grow when northern summers are too cool to melt the winter's snow.

cards.headline: Proof from the seafloor
cards.body: In 1976 a study titled 'Pacemaker of the Ice Ages' read deep-sea sediment cores covering 450,000 years, and the big climate swings matched the orbital cycles. A key clue: oxygen isotopes in the shells of foraminifera, single-celled sea creatures whose shells pile up into limestone and chalk. Ice ages once came about every 41,000 years; about 800,000 years ago the beat stretched to 100,000, and scientists still aren't sure why.

cards.headline: Orbital cycles: timed
learned: Orbit shape, tilt and wobble change slowly
Cool northern summers let ice sheets grow
Growing ice reflects sunlight and cools more
Seafloor shells confirmed the theory in 1976

questions.prompt: The orbital cycle that is a change in the tilt of Earth's axis is called _____.

options.label: eccentricity
options.rationale: That's the shape of the orbit.

options.label: precession
options.rationale: That's the wobble of the axis.

options.label: revolution
options.rationale: That's one trip around the Sun, not a slow cycle.

questions.explanation: Obliquity is the tilt, which swings between 22.1° and 24.5° over about 41,000 years.

questions.prompt: Match each orbital cycle with what it describes.
questions.explanation: Eccentricity is the shape of Earth's orbit, obliquity is the tilt of the axis, and precession is a wobble of the axis, like a top.

questions.prompt: The 1976 study read foraminifera shells from deep-sea mud. Which rock can such piles of shells become?

options.label: Sandstone
options.rationale: Sandstone is cemented sand grains, not shells.

questions.explanation: Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate, often from fossil shells of sea life, and foraminifera shells help build it.
